A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same gradient-inversion poisoning work. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the changed title and layout.

before.justification: v1 reports original CIFAR-10 poisoning experiments with CNN and ViT models, including accuracy, training slowdown, and poison-selection results in the main text and appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains the original CIFAR-10 experiments and adds original results from a synthetic XOR poisoning experiment in Section 5.1.

M1.justification: The gradient-inversion procedure, GA/OG/LIE objectives, adaptive LIE construction, and Adam optimization with feasibility clipping remain unchanged. Expanded explanations and the separate XOR demonstration do not revise the proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 adds synthetic two-dimensional XOR classification and a single poisoned-update scenario in Section 5.1. This is a limited illustrative extension beyond the retained CIFAR-10 coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding CIFAR-10 comparisons retain GA, OG, LIE, their poisoning counterparts, and clean/random-poison controls. The XOR demonstration includes a chance-accuracy reference but does not evaluate an additional comparator against the proposed inversion method.

E3.justification: The added XOR experiment trains an MLP using full-batch gradient descent on 1,000 points, then evaluates one contaminated update using repeated copies of a candidate poison. The reported CIFAR-10 training budgets, model configurations, contamination settings, and evaluation procedures remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 Figure 4 adds accuracy landscapes over poison locations and a sensitivity curve over contamination levels, examining damage from a single poisoned update. Existing analyses of feasible sets, optimizers, aggregation, early stopping, and architecture are retained.

E5.justification: The retained experiments still report four runs with different initializations and splits, standard errors on plots, and standard deviations for poison-selection rates. The XOR addition specifies no new repeated-run or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: v2 Figure 4 adds XOR results, including minimum accuracy around 54% after one poisoned update at 10% contamination, close to the 50% chance reference. Existing CIFAR-10 numerical tables and plotted results, including those in the appendices, are unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives, attack formulas, and substantive assumptions are retained. Revised notation and the explicit gradient-matching equation restate the existing formulation; the added dimensionality discussion is intuitive explanation, without a new theorem, proof, or formal guarantee.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains demonstrating availability attacks on nonconvex neural networks through gradient-inverted data poisoning. The worst-case qualification and 1% contamination result highlighted in v2's abstract were already present in v1's conclusion and Section 5.2.

C2.justification: v2 adds an input-dimensionality/nonlinearity explanation for restricted poisoning expressivity and cautions that XOR may exaggerate label-flipping effects. Section 5.2 also changes the gradient-attack upper-bound interpretation from an assertion to an expectation. Existing practical limitations remain.

D1.justification: Section 5.1 documents the XOR labeling rule, regular poison-grid sampling, label flipping, and repetition to reach the chosen contamination level. These provide reproducibility information for the added experiment. Existing CNN architecture and CIFAR-10 implementation disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hardt et al. (2023), Algorithmic Collective Action in Machine Learning, to the defense discussion. It also explicitly relates iterative poisoning to Steinhardt et al.'s Algorithm 1 and clarifies connections to Farhadkhani et al.'s threat model, without substantially changing the overall positioning.

P1.justification: The title and author information change, and the abstract, framework, and method receive explanatory edits. Experiments gain a preliminary subsection and separate gradient-attack/data-poisoning result headings. The main narrative and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation, substantially resizing and repositioning figures and tables. v2 adds the XOR figure, moves v1's appendix Table 4 into the main text as Table 2, and rearranges appendix panels, including a two-row layout for Figure 10. Existing plots retain their content.

improvement.justification: v2 clarifies the message-based threat model and poisoning expressivity, adds a cautiously interpreted single-update XOR illustration, and places the gradient-attack results beside their discussion. These modestly improve explanation and accessibility while preserving the original evidence. The XOR study does not substantially strengthen validation of the inversion method or resolve the existing practical limitations.
